description: Sentence Transformation question bank for FDA & SDA Competitive Examination. Covers all topics from the provided study notes: affirmative/negative/interrogative/exclamatory transformations; simple, compound and complex sentences; clauses; conjunctions; non-finite forms; degree and emphasis patterns; punctuation; common errors; and practice questions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a sentence?

options.A: A group of words that expresses a complete thought and normally contains a finite verb
options.B: A group of words without any verb
options.C: A group of words that always contains a non-finite verb
options.D: A group of words that cannot stand alone

questions.explanation: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought and normally contains a finite verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is sentence transformation?

options.A: Changing the meaning of a sentence completely
options.B: Changing the grammatical structure or form of a sentence without changing its essential meaning
options.C: Translating a sentence into another language
options.D: Removing all verbs from a sentence

questions.explanation: Sentence transformation means changing the grammatical structure or form of a sentence without changing its essential meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a finite verb?

options.A: A verb form that does not show tense
options.B: A verb that is marked for tense and/or agrees with its subject
options.C: A verb ending in -ing used as a noun
options.D: A verb preceded by 'to'

questions.explanation: A finite verb is marked for tense and/or agrees with its subject, e.g. writes, wrote, is, have.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a non-finite verb?

options.A: A verb that independently shows tense and subject agreement
options.B: A verb form that does not independently show tense or subject agreement
options.C: A verb that always ends in -ed
options.D: A verb that must have a subject

questions.explanation: A non-finite verb does not independently show tense or subject agreement, e.g. to write, writing, written.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an affirmative sentence?

options.A: A sentence that asks a question
options.B: A sentence that expresses denial
options.C: A sentence that states or asserts something positively
options.D: A sentence that expresses strong feeling

questions.explanation: An affirmative sentence states or asserts something positively, e.g. 'She is honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a negative sentence?

options.A: A sentence that states something positively
options.B: A sentence that expresses denial or negation
options.C: A sentence that asks a question
options.D: A sentence that expresses strong emotion

questions.explanation: A negative sentence expresses denial or negation, e.g. 'She is not dishonest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an interrogative sentence?

options.A: A sentence that states a fact
options.B: A sentence that expresses strong feeling
options.C: A sentence that asks a question
options.D: A sentence that contains a dependent clause

questions.explanation: An interrogative sentence asks a question, e.g. 'Is she honest?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an exclamatory sentence?

options.A: A sentence that expresses strong feeling such as joy, sorrow, surprise or admiration
options.B: A sentence that asks a question
options.C: A sentence that states a fact neutrally
options.D: A sentence with two independent clauses

questions.explanation: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling such as joy, sorrow, surprise or admiration, e.g. 'What a beautiful day!'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a simple sentence?

options.A: A sentence with two or more independent clauses
options.B: A sentence with one independent clause and one finite verb group
options.C: A sentence with one main clause and at least one dependent clause
options.D: A sentence without any verb

questions.explanation: A simple sentence has one independent clause and one finite verb group, though it may contain non-finite phrases and multiple objects or modifiers.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a compound sentence?

options.A: A sentence with one independent clause
options.B: A sentence containing two or more independent clauses, commonly joined by coordinating conjunctions
options.C: A sentence with one main clause and one dependent clause
options.D: A sentence with only non-finite verbs

questions.explanation: A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses, commonly joined by coordinating conjunctions or suitable punctuation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a complex sentence?

options.A: A sentence with only one independent clause
options.B: A sentence with two independent clauses joined by 'and'
options.C: A sentence containing one independent clause and at least one dependent clause
options.D: A sentence with no finite verb

questions.explanation: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an independent clause?

options.A: A clause that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence
options.B: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence
options.C: A phrase without a verb
options.D: A clause introduced only by 'because'

questions.explanation: An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a dependent clause?

options.A: A clause that can always stand alone
options.B: A clause that cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence and depends on another clause
options.C: A group of words without a subject
options.D: A sentence with two independent clauses

questions.explanation: A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence and depends on another clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is an affirmative sentence changed into a negative sentence?

options.A: By removing the subject
options.B: By introducing an appropriate negative construction while preserving the original meaning
options.C: By changing the tense to past
options.D: By adding an exclamation mark

questions.explanation: An affirmative sentence is changed into a negative sentence by introducing an appropriate negative construction, often with not, never, no, nobody, nothing or an equivalent expression, while preserving the original meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into negative without changing meaning: 'Everyone was present.'

options.A: No one was absent.
options.B: Everyone was not present.
options.C: Someone was absent.
options.D: No one was present.

questions.explanation: 'Everyone was present' is logically equivalent to 'No one was absent' in the intended context.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into negative construction: 'Only Ravi can solve this problem.'

options.A: Ravi cannot solve this problem.
options.B: None but Ravi can solve this problem.
options.C: Everyone can solve this problem.
options.D: No one can solve this problem.

questions.explanation: 'Only Ravi can solve this problem' becomes 'None but Ravi can solve this problem' — a formal examination-style negative equivalent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change using 'never': 'He is always punctual.'

options.A: He is never punctual.
options.B: He is never late.
options.C: He is not always late.
options.D: He is sometimes late.

questions.explanation: 'He is always punctual' is equivalent to 'He is never late.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change using 'no sooner': 'As soon as the bell rang, the students left.'

options.A: No sooner the bell rang than the students left.
options.B: No sooner had the bell rung than the students left.
options.C: No sooner did the bell ring when the students left.
options.D: No sooner the bell had rung when the students left.

questions.explanation: 'As soon as the bell rang, the students left' becomes 'No sooner had the bell rung than the students left.' The structure is: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change using 'hardly': 'As soon as he arrived, it began to rain.'

options.A: Hardly had he arrived than it began to rain.
options.B: Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain.
options.C: Hardly he arrived when it began to rain.
options.D: Hardly did he arrive than it began to rain.

questions.explanation: 'As soon as he arrived, it began to rain' becomes 'Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain.' Hardly/scarcely pair with 'when', not 'than'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into negative form: 'He is too weak to walk.'

options.A: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
options.B: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
options.C: He is not weak to walk.
options.D: He is weak enough to walk.

questions.explanation: 'Too + adjective + to-infinitive' becomes 'so + adjective + that + subject + cannot + verb': 'He is too weak to walk' → 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform: 'The box is too heavy for me to lift.'

options.A: The box is so heavy that I cannot lift it.
options.B: The box is too heavy that I cannot lift.
options.C: The box is not heavy for me to lift.
options.D: The box is heavy enough for me to lift.

questions.explanation: 'Too heavy for me to lift' becomes 'so heavy that I cannot lift it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform into affirmative: 'He is not a fool.'

options.A: He is wise / He is sensible.
options.B: He is a fool.
options.C: He is very foolish.
options.D: He is not wise.

questions.explanation: 'He is not a fool' can be transformed affirmatively as 'He is wise / He is sensible.' The best equivalent depends on the intended meaning; 'not a fool' does not always mean 'wise.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform affirmatively: 'Nobody can deny the truth.'

options.A: Everybody must accept the truth.
options.B: Somebody can deny the truth.
options.C: Nobody accepts the truth.
options.D: Everybody can deny the truth.

questions.explanation: 'Nobody can deny the truth' becomes 'Everybody must accept the truth' — a contextual equivalent, not a word-for-word substitution.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform affirmatively: 'He never tells lies.'

options.A: He always speaks the truth.
options.B: He sometimes tells lies.
options.C: He never speaks the truth.
options.D: He often tells lies.

questions.explanation: 'He never tells lies' is equivalent to 'He always speaks the truth.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform affirmatively: 'No other metal is as useful as iron.'

options.A: Iron is the most useful metal.
options.B: Iron is less useful than other metals.
options.C: No metal is useful.
options.D: Iron is not useful.

questions.explanation: 'No other metal is as useful as iron' becomes 'Iron is the most useful metal' — this uses a superlative comparison.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform negatively: 'Very few cities are as large as Mumbai.'

options.A: Many cities are not as large as Mumbai.
options.B: No city is as large as Mumbai.
options.C: All cities are as large as Mumbai.
options.D: Mumbai is not a large city.

questions.explanation: 'Very few cities are as large as Mumbai' becomes 'Many cities are not as large as Mumbai.' The exact equivalent depends on the comparison set; preserve the intended degree.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'not all' and 'none'?

options.A: They mean the same thing.
options.B: Not all means some may not; none means not even one.
options.C: None means some may not; not all means not even one.
options.D: Both mean everyone.

questions.explanation: 'Not all' means some may not; 'none' means not even one. They are not interchangeable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the danger of using double negatives?

options.A: They always create emphasis.
options.B: Two negatives may create a positive or nonstandard meaning.
options.C: They are always grammatically correct.
options.D: They make a sentence interrogative.

questions.explanation: Two negatives may create a positive or nonstandard meaning: 'I don't know nothing' is generally incorrect in standard exam English; use 'I don't know anything.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'Too...to' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: So...that...cannot/could not
options.B: Not only...but also
options.C: No sooner...than
options.D: None but

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'Too...to' becomes 'So...that...cannot/could not'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'As soon as...' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: No sooner...than / Hardly...when
options.B: So...that...cannot
options.C: None but
options.D: Not all

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'As soon as...' becomes 'No sooner...than / Hardly...when'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'Only' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: None but / nothing but / no more than, according to meaning
options.B: Never
options.C: Not all
options.D: Cannot but

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'Only' becomes 'None but / nothing but / no more than, according to meaning'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'Must' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: Cannot but / cannot help but (only where meaning fits)
options.B: None but
options.C: No sooner...than
options.D: Never

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'Must' becomes 'Cannot but / cannot help but (only where meaning fits)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'Both...and' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: Not only...but also (not always exact in emphasis)
options.B: None but
options.C: So...that...cannot
options.D: No sooner...than

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'Both...and' becomes 'Not only...but also (not always exact in emphasis)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'All are not...' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: Not all... (partial negation; not none)
options.B: None...
options.C: No one...
options.D: Never...

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'All are not...' becomes 'Not all... (partial negation; not none)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How can an affirmative statement be transformed into an interrogative sentence without changing its meaning?

options.A: By using a rhetorical question or a question form that conveys the same assertion
options.B: By adding 'not' to the sentence
options.C: By changing it into an exclamatory sentence
options.D: By removing the subject

questions.explanation: An affirmative statement can be transformed into an interrogative sentence by using a rhetorical question or a question form that conveys the same assertion: 'Everyone wants to be happy' → 'Who does not want to be happy?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform interrogatively: 'No one can deny the importance of education.'

options.A: Who can deny the importance of education?
options.B: Can no one deny the importance of education?
options.C: Why can no one deny the importance of education?
options.D: Who cannot deny the importance of education?

questions.explanation: 'No one can deny the importance of education' becomes 'Who can deny the importance of education?' — a rhetorical question whose expected answer is nobody.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform interrogatively: 'It is useless to cry over spilt milk.'

options.A: What is the use of crying over spilt milk?
options.B: Why is it useful to cry over spilt milk?
options.C: Is it useless to cry over spilt milk?
options.D: Who cries over spilt milk?

questions.explanation: 'It is useless to cry over spilt milk' becomes 'What is the use of crying over spilt milk?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform interrogatively: 'There is no use in arguing with him.'

options.A: What is the use of arguing with him?
options.B: Why argue with him?
options.C: Is there no use in arguing with him?
options.D: Who argues with him?

questions.explanation: 'There is no use in arguing with him' becomes 'What is the use of arguing with him?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform interrogatively: 'Everyone loves freedom.'

options.A: Who does not love freedom?
options.B: Does everyone love freedom?
options.C: Who loves freedom?
options.D: Why does everyone love freedom?

questions.explanation: 'Everyone loves freedom' becomes 'Who does not love freedom?' — a rhetorical question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform interrogatively: 'Only a brave person can do this.'

options.A: Who but a brave person can do this?
options.B: Can a brave person do this?
options.C: Who can do this?
options.D: Why can only a brave person do this?

questions.explanation: 'Only a brave person can do this' becomes 'Who but a brave person can do this?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform interrogatively: 'A wise person would never act so foolishly.'

options.A: Would a wise person ever act so foolishly?
options.B: Would a wise person never act so foolishly?
options.C: Why would a wise person act so foolishly?
options.D: Does a wise person act so foolishly?

questions.explanation: 'A wise person would never act so foolishly' becomes 'Would a wise person ever act so foolishly?' — a rhetorical question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform into an affirmative statement: 'Can anyone forget the sacrifice of our soldiers?'

options.A: No one can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.
options.B: Everyone can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.
options.C: Anyone can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.
options.D: Someone can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.

questions.explanation: 'Can anyone forget the sacrifice of our soldiers?' becomes 'No one can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a rhetorical question?

options.A: A question asked to obtain information
options.B: A question asked for emphasis or effect, not to obtain information
options.C: A question that always expects a 'yes' answer
options.D: A question that cannot be transformed

questions.explanation: A rhetorical question is asked for emphasis or effect, not to obtain information. Its implied answer is generally understood.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is an exclamatory sentence changed into an assertive sentence?

options.A: By adding an exclamation mark
options.B: By removing the exclamatory form and expressing the same feeling as a statement
options.C: By changing it into a question
options.D: By removing the subject

questions.explanation: An exclamatory sentence is changed into an assertive sentence by removing the exclamatory form and expressing the same feeling as a statement, often using very, greatly, extremely or a suitable descriptive phrase.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'What a beautiful flower it is!'

options.A: It is a very beautiful flower.
options.B: What a flower it is.
options.C: The flower is beautiful.
options.D: Is it a beautiful flower?

questions.explanation: 'What a beautiful flower it is!' becomes 'It is a very beautiful flower.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'How clever she is!'

options.A: She is very clever.
options.B: How is she clever?
options.C: She is not clever.
options.D: She is clever.

questions.explanation: 'How clever she is!' becomes 'She is very clever.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'Alas! He is dead.'

options.A: It is very sad that he is dead.
options.B: He is dead.
options.C: Is he dead?
options.D: He is not dead.

questions.explanation: 'Alas! He is dead' becomes 'It is very sad that he is dead.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'Hurrah! We have won the match.'

options.A: We are very happy that we have won the match.
options.B: We have won the match.
options.C: Have we won the match?
options.D: We have not won the match.

questions.explanation: 'Hurrah! We have won the match' becomes 'We are very happy that we have won the match.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'What a pity!'

options.A: It is a great pity.
options.B: It is a pity.
options.C: Is it a pity?
options.D: It is not a pity.

questions.explanation: 'What a pity!' becomes 'It is a great pity.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'Would that I were a king!'

options.A: I wish that I were a king.
options.B: I am a king.
options.C: Am I a king?
options.D: I am not a king.

questions.explanation: 'Would that I were a king!' becomes 'I wish that I were a king.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Express as an assertive sentence: 'If only I could fly!'

options.A: I wish I could fly.
options.B: I can fly.
options.C: Can I fly?
options.D: I cannot fly.

questions.explanation: 'If only I could fly!' becomes 'I wish I could fly.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive form: 'May you live long!'

options.A: I wish that you may live long / I hope that you live long.
options.B: You live long.
options.C: Will you live long?
options.D: You do not live long.

questions.explanation: 'May you live long!' becomes 'I wish that you may live long / I hope that you live long.' Choose the construction that preserves the blessing or wish.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which words commonly introduce exclamations?

options.A: What, how, alas, hurrah, bravo, oh, ah
options.B: Because, although, if, when
options.C: And, but, or, so
options.D: Who, whom, whose, which

questions.explanation: Words commonly introducing exclamations include what, how, alas, hurrah, bravo, oh, ah and expressions such as would that and if only.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What punctuation normally ends an exclamatory sentence?

options.A: A full stop
options.B: A question mark
options.C: An exclamation mark (!)
options.D: A semicolon

questions.explanation: An exclamatory sentence normally ends with an exclamation mark (!). An assertive transformation normally ends with a full stop.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A simple sentence may contain which of the following?

options.A: Two independent clauses
options.B: One independent clause with additional phrases or non-finite constructions
options.C: One main clause and one dependent clause
options.D: Only a dependent clause

questions.explanation: A simple sentence has one independent clause. It may contain a subject, one finite predicate and additional phrases or non-finite constructions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A compound sentence has at least how many independent clauses?

options.A: One
options.B: Two
options.C: Three
options.D: Zero

questions.explanation: A compound sentence has at least two independent clauses joined by a coordinator or suitable punctuation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A complex sentence has one independent clause and how many dependent clauses?

options.A: Zero
options.B: At least one
options.C: Exactly two
options.D: No dependent clause

questions.explanation: A complex sentence has one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the three main clause types relevant to sentence structure?

options.A: Independent clause, noun clause and adjective/relative clause
options.B: Noun clause, adjective/relative clause and adverb clause
options.C: Independent clause, dependent clause and phrase
options.D: Main clause, subordinate clause and coordinate clause

questions.explanation: The three main clause types relevant to sentence structure are noun clause, adjective/relative clause and adverb clause. Noun, adjective and adverb clauses are dependent clause types. (Independent clause is a clause type but the notes list the three dependent clause types as noun, adjective and adverb.)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are coordinating conjunctions?

options.A: Conjunctions joining elements of unequal grammatical rank
options.B: Conjunctions joining elements of equal grammatical rank
options.C: Words introducing dependent clauses
options.D: Words that replace nouns

questions.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions join elements of equal grammatical rank: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a list of coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS)?

options.A: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
options.B: because, although, if, when, while, since, unless
options.C: who, whom, whose, which, that
options.D: before, after, though, since, until

questions.explanation: FANBOYS stands for for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — the coordinating conjunctions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are subordinating conjunctions?

options.A: Words joining elements of equal rank
options.B: Words introducing dependent clauses
options.C: Words that replace nouns
options.D: Words that express strong feeling

questions.explanation: Subordinating conjunctions are words introducing dependent clauses, such as because, although, if, when, while, since, unless, before, after and though.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a phrase?

options.A: A group of words containing a subject and a predicate
options.B: A group of words functioning as a unit but not containing a finite subject-verb clause
options.C: A group of words that always contains a finite verb
options.D: A complete sentence

questions.explanation: A phrase is a group of words functioning as a unit but not containing a finite subject-verb clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a clause?

options.A: A group of words without a verb
options.B: A group of words containing a subject and a predicate
options.C: A group of words that always ends with an exclamation mark
options.D: A single word

questions.explanation: A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a predicate; a finite clause has a finite verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a simple sentence contain more than one verb?

options.A: No, a simple sentence has only one verb.
options.B: Yes, it may contain a compound predicate or non-finite verb forms while still having one independent clause.
options.C: Yes, but only if it has two independent clauses.
options.D: No, because a simple sentence has no verb.

questions.explanation: A simple sentence may contain more than one verb — it may contain a compound predicate or non-finite verb forms, while still having one independent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a compound sentence contain a dependent clause?

options.A: No, a compound sentence never contains a dependent clause.
options.B: Yes, a sentence may be compound-complex.
options.C: Only if it has three independent clauses.
options.D: Only if it has no coordinating conjunction.

questions.explanation: Yes, a sentence may be compound-complex. A compound sentence in the basic classification has two or more independent clauses; additional dependent clauses can also occur.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'He worked hard to pass.'

options.A: He worked hard, and he passed.
options.B: He worked hard because he passed.
options.C: He worked hard although he passed.
options.D: He worked hard to pass.

questions.explanation: 'He worked hard to pass' becomes 'He worked hard, and he passed.' This is a contextual transformation; the result should preserve purpose/result as closely as possible.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'In spite of his poverty, he is honest.'

options.A: He is poor, but he is honest.
options.B: He is poor, so he is honest.
options.C: He is poor, and he is honest.
options.D: He is poor, or he is honest.

questions.explanation: 'In spite of his poverty, he is honest' becomes 'He is poor, but he is honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Being tired, she went to bed.'

options.A: She was tired, so she went to bed.
options.B: She was tired, but she went to bed.
options.C: She was tired, and she went to bed.
options.D: She was tired, or she went to bed.

questions.explanation: 'Being tired, she went to bed' becomes 'She was tired, so she went to bed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'On seeing the police, the thief ran away.'

options.A: The thief saw the police, and he ran away.
options.B: The thief saw the police, but he ran away.
options.C: The thief saw the police, so he ran away.
options.D: The thief saw the police, or he ran away.

questions.explanation: 'On seeing the police, the thief ran away' becomes 'The thief saw the police, and he ran away.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Besides being intelligent, she is hardworking.'

options.A: She is intelligent, and she is also hardworking.
options.B: She is intelligent, but she is hardworking.
options.C: She is intelligent, so she is hardworking.
options.D: She is intelligent, or she is hardworking.

questions.explanation: 'Besides being intelligent, she is hardworking' becomes 'She is intelligent, and she is also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'To avoid punishment, he confessed.'

options.A: He wanted to avoid punishment, so he confessed.
options.B: He wanted to avoid punishment, but he confessed.
options.C: He wanted to avoid punishment, and he confessed.
options.D: He wanted to avoid punishment, or he confessed.

questions.explanation: 'To avoid punishment, he confessed' becomes 'He wanted to avoid punishment, so he confessed.' The exact causal relation should be preserved.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Without working hard, you cannot succeed.'

options.A: Work hard, or you cannot succeed.
options.B: Work hard, and you cannot succeed.
options.C: Work hard, so you cannot succeed.
options.D: Work hard, but you cannot succeed.

questions.explanation: 'Without working hard, you cannot succeed' becomes 'Work hard, or you cannot succeed.' This is an equivalent warning/advice construction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What should be checked in simple-to-compound transformation?

options.A: Only the punctuation
options.B: Ensure each independent clause has a complete subject-finite verb structure and use a coordinator that reflects the original relation
options.C: Only the number of words
options.D: Only the tense of the first clause

questions.explanation: In simple-to-compound transformation, ensure each independent clause has a complete subject-finite verb structure and use a coordinator that reflects the original relation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple using a participle: 'He finished his work, and he went home.'

options.A: Having finished his work, he went home.
options.B: He finished his work and went home.
options.C: After he finished his work, he went home.
options.D: He finished his work, so he went home.

questions.explanation: 'He finished his work, and he went home' becomes 'Having finished his work, he went home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple: 'He was ill, but he attended the meeting.'

options.A: In spite of being ill, he attended the meeting.
options.B: Because he was ill, he attended the meeting.
options.C: He was ill and attended the meeting.
options.D: If he was ill, he attended the meeting.

questions.explanation: 'He was ill, but he attended the meeting' becomes 'In spite of being ill, he attended the meeting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple: 'The sun set, and we returned home.'

options.A: The sun having set, we returned home / At sunset, we returned home.
options.B: The sun set and we returned home.
options.C: When the sun set, we returned home.
options.D: Because the sun set, we returned home.

questions.explanation: 'The sun set, and we returned home' becomes 'The sun having set, we returned home / At sunset, we returned home.' Choose according to the intended time relation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple: 'He took a taxi, so he reached on time.'

options.A: By taking a taxi, he reached on time.
options.B: He took a taxi and reached on time.
options.C: Because he took a taxi, he reached on time.
options.D: If he took a taxi, he reached on time.

questions.explanation: 'He took a taxi, so he reached on time' becomes 'By taking a taxi, he reached on time.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple: 'She was poor, but she was generous.'

options.A: In spite of her poverty, she was generous.
options.B: Because she was poor, she was generous.
options.C: She was poor and generous.
options.D: If she was poor, she was generous.

questions.explanation: 'She was poor, but she was generous' becomes 'In spite of her poverty, she was generous.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple: 'He saw the snake and ran away.'

options.A: On seeing the snake, he ran away.
options.B: Because he saw the snake, he ran away.
options.C: Although he saw the snake, he ran away.
options.D: If he saw the snake, he ran away.

questions.explanation: 'He saw the snake and ran away' becomes 'On seeing the snake, he ran away.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a participial phrase?

options.A: A phrase built around a present or past participle
options.B: A phrase headed by an -ing form functioning as a noun
options.C: A phrase built around 'to + base verb'
options.D: A phrase containing a finite verb

questions.explanation: A participial phrase is a phrase built around a present or past participle, such as 'seeing the teacher' or 'having completed the task'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a gerund phrase?

options.A: A phrase built around a present or past participle
options.B: A phrase headed by an -ing form functioning as a noun
options.C: A phrase built around 'to + base verb'
options.D: A phrase with a finite verb

questions.explanation: A gerund phrase is a phrase headed by an -ing form functioning as a noun: 'Swimming every day is healthy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an infinitive phrase?

options.A: A phrase built around a present or past participle
options.B: A phrase headed by an -ing form functioning as a noun
options.C: A phrase built around 'to + base verb', often expressing purpose
options.D: A phrase containing a finite verb

questions.explanation: An infinitive phrase is built around to + base verb, often expressing purpose: 'To win the prize, she practised daily.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex using 'because': 'Being ill, he stayed home.'

options.A: Because he was ill, he stayed home.
options.B: Although he was ill, he stayed home.
options.C: If he was ill, he stayed home.
options.D: When he was ill, he stayed home.

questions.explanation: 'Being ill, he stayed home' becomes 'Because he was ill, he stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'In spite of his hard work, he failed.'

options.A: Although he worked hard, he failed.
options.B: Because he worked hard, he failed.
options.C: If he worked hard, he failed.
options.D: When he worked hard, he failed.

questions.explanation: 'In spite of his hard work, he failed' becomes 'Although he worked hard, he failed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'On hearing the news, she fainted.'

options.A: When she heard the news, she fainted.
options.B: Although she heard the news, she fainted.
options.C: If she heard the news, she fainted.
options.D: Because she heard the news, she fainted.

questions.explanation: 'On hearing the news, she fainted' becomes 'When she heard the news, she fainted.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'I know him to be honest.'

options.A: I know that he is honest.
options.B: I know him although he is honest.
options.C: I know him if he is honest.
options.D: I know him when he is honest.

questions.explanation: 'I know him to be honest' becomes 'I know that he is honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'The man standing there is my uncle.'

options.A: The man who is standing there is my uncle.
options.B: The man although standing there is my uncle.
options.C: The man if standing there is my uncle.
options.D: The man when standing there is my uncle.

questions.explanation: 'The man standing there is my uncle' becomes 'The man who is standing there is my uncle.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'He is too weak to walk.'

options.A: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
options.B: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
options.C: He is weak although he cannot walk.
options.D: He is weak if he cannot walk.

questions.explanation: 'He is too weak to walk' becomes 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'Despite being rich, he is unhappy.'

options.A: Although he is rich, he is unhappy.
options.B: Because he is rich, he is unhappy.
options.C: If he is rich, he is unhappy.
options.D: When he is rich, he is unhappy.

questions.explanation: 'Despite being rich, he is unhappy' becomes 'Although he is rich, he is unhappy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'In the event of rain, the match will be cancelled.'

options.A: If it rains, the match will be cancelled.
options.B: Although it rains, the match will be cancelled.
options.C: When it rains, the match will be cancelled.
options.D: Because it rains, the match will be cancelled.

questions.explanation: 'In the event of rain, the match will be cancelled' becomes 'If it rains, the match will be cancelled.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the role of a relative clause in transformation?

options.A: It qualifies a noun
options.B: It functions as a noun
options.C: It expresses time, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result, place or manner
options.D: It joins two independent clauses

questions.explanation: A relative clause qualifies a noun: 'The girl wearing a red dress' → 'The girl who is wearing a red dress.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the role of a noun clause?

options.A: It qualifies a noun
options.B: It functions as a noun
options.C: It expresses time, reason or condition
options.D: It joins two independent clauses

questions.explanation: A noun clause functions as a noun: 'I know his address' → 'I know where he lives' (meaning must be kept appropriately).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the role of an adverb clause?

options.A: It qualifies a noun
options.B: It functions as a noun
options.C: It expresses time, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result, place or manner
options.D: It joins two independent clauses

questions.explanation: An adverb clause expresses time, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result, place or manner.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound using 'so': 'As he was ill, he stayed home.'

options.A: He was ill, so he stayed home.
options.B: He was ill, but he stayed home.
options.C: He was ill, and he stayed home.
options.D: He was ill, or he stayed home.

questions.explanation: 'As he was ill, he stayed home' becomes 'He was ill, so he stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Though he is poor, he is honest.'

options.A: He is poor, but he is honest.
options.B: He is poor, so he is honest.
options.C: He is poor, and he is honest.
options.D: He is poor, or he is honest.

questions.explanation: 'Though he is poor, he is honest' becomes 'He is poor, but he is honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'If you work hard, you will succeed.'

options.A: Work hard, and you will succeed.
options.B: Work hard, or you will succeed.
options.C: Work hard, but you will succeed.
options.D: Work hard, so you will succeed.

questions.explanation: 'If you work hard, you will succeed' becomes 'Work hard, and you will succeed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.'

options.A: Hurry, or you will miss the bus.
options.B: Hurry, and you will miss the bus.
options.C: Hurry, but you will miss the bus.
options.D: Hurry, so you will miss the bus.

questions.explanation: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus' becomes 'Hurry, or you will miss the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'When the bell rang, the students left.'

options.A: The bell rang, and then the students left.
options.B: The bell rang, but the students left.
options.C: The bell rang, or the students left.
options.D: The bell rang, so the students left.

questions.explanation: 'When the bell rang, the students left' becomes 'The bell rang, and then the students left.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

options.A: He is very weak, and he cannot walk.
options.B: He is very weak, but he cannot walk.
options.C: He is very weak, or he cannot walk.
options.D: He is very weak, so he cannot walk.

questions.explanation: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk' becomes 'He is very weak, and he cannot walk.' This preserves the basic result, though the exact emphasis may differ.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Although she was tired, she continued working.'

options.A: She was tired, but she continued working.
options.B: She was tired, so she continued working.
options.C: She was tired, and she continued working.
options.D: She was tired, or she continued working.

questions.explanation: 'Although she was tired, she continued working' becomes 'She was tired, but she continued working.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Because he was careless, he made a mistake.'

options.A: He was careless, so he made a mistake.
options.B: He was careless, but he made a mistake.
options.C: He was careless, and he made a mistake.
options.D: He was careless, or he made a mistake.

questions.explanation: 'Because he was careless, he made a mistake' becomes 'He was careless, so he made a mistake.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses reason/result?

options.A: because / since / as
options.B: although / though / even though
options.C: if
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Reason/result is expressed by because / since / as in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is so / therefore.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses contrast/concession?

options.A: because / since / as
options.B: although / though / even though
options.C: if
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Contrast/concession is expressed by although / though / even though in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is but / yet / still.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses condition?

options.A: because
options.B: although
options.C: if
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Condition is expressed by 'if' in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is 'and (imperative + and)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses negative condition?

options.A: because
options.B: although
options.C: if
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Negative condition is expressed by 'unless' in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is 'or / otherwise'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses time?

options.A: when / after / before
options.B: because / since / as
options.C: although / though
options.D: so that / in order that

questions.explanation: Time is expressed by when / after / before in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is 'and then / and'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses purpose?

options.A: because
options.B: so that / in order that
options.C: although
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Purpose is expressed by so that / in order that in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is 'and so / imperative + and (contextual)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses result?

options.A: so...that
options.B: because
options.C: although
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Result is expressed by so...that in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is 'and therefore / and'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which complex connector expresses concession?

options.A: because
options.B: even though
options.C: if
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: Concession is expressed by even though in complex constructions; the compound equivalent is 'but / yet'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Are connectors in the conjunction and connector pairs table universally interchangeable?

options.A: Yes, any connector can replace any other.
options.B: No. Select the connector that preserves the exact logical relation.
options.C: Yes, because all connectors express the same meaning.
options.D: No, because connectors have no meaning.

questions.explanation: Connectors in the table are not universally interchangeable. Select the connector that preserves the exact logical relation — cause, result, contrast, concession, condition or time.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'too...to' transformed?

options.A: Too + adjective/adverb + to-infinitive becomes so + adjective/adverb + that + subject + cannot/could not + verb
options.B: Too + adjective becomes very + adjective
options.C: Too + adjective becomes enough + adjective
options.D: Too + adjective becomes not + adjective

questions.explanation: Too + adjective/adverb + to-infinitive often becomes so + adjective/adverb + that + subject + cannot/could not + verb: 'He is too weak to walk' → 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'enough to' transformed?

options.A: Adjective/adverb + enough + to-infinitive becomes so + adjective/adverb + that + subject + can/could
options.B: Enough + to becomes too + to
options.C: Enough + to becomes not + enough
options.D: Enough + to becomes very + adjective

questions.explanation: Adjective/adverb + enough + to-infinitive can become so + adjective/adverb + that + subject + can/could: 'She is strong enough to lift it' → 'She is so strong that she can lift it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'as soon as' transformed?

options.A: As soon as + clause can become no sooner...than or hardly/scarcely...when
options.B: As soon as + clause can become so...that
options.C: As soon as + clause can become too...to
options.D: As soon as + clause can become unless

questions.explanation: 'As soon as' + clause can become no sooner...than or hardly/scarcely...when: 'As soon as he arrived, we left' → 'No sooner had he arrived than we left.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the structure of 'no sooner'?

options.A: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple
options.B: No sooner + subject + had + past participle + when + past simple
options.C: No sooner + did + subject + past participle + than + past simple
options.D: No sooner + has + subject + past participle + than + past simple

questions.explanation: The structure is: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple: 'No sooner had I reached than it began to rain.' More idiomatically: 'No sooner had I arrived than it began to rain.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the structure of 'hardly/scarcely'?

options.A: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when/before + past simple
options.B: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple
options.C: Hardly/Scarcely + did + subject + past participle + when + past simple
options.D: Hardly/Scarcely + has + subject + past participle + than + past simple

questions.explanation: The structure is: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when/before + past simple.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'unless' transformed?

options.A: Unless means if...not
options.B: Unless means if...also
options.C: Unless means because
options.D: Unless means although

questions.explanation: Unless means if...not: 'Unless you study, you will fail' → 'If you do not study, you will fail.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'in spite of' transformed?

options.A: In spite of/despite + noun or gerund can become although/though + clause
options.B: In spite of + noun can become because + clause
options.C: In spite of + noun can become if + clause
options.D: In spite of + noun can become unless + clause

questions.explanation: In spite of/despite + noun or gerund can become although/though + clause: 'Despite the rain, we played' → 'Although it was raining, we played.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'because of' transformed?

options.A: Because of + noun/gerund can become because + clause
options.B: Because of + noun can become although + clause
options.C: Because of + noun can become if + clause
options.D: Because of + noun can become unless + clause

questions.explanation: Because of + noun/gerund can become because + clause: 'Because of his illness, he was absent' → 'Because he was ill, he was absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'without' transformed?

options.A: Without + gerund/noun can often become if...not or unless
options.B: Without + gerund can become although
options.C: Without + gerund can become because
options.D: Without + gerund can become so...that

questions.explanation: Without + gerund/noun can often become if...not or unless: 'Without water, plants die' → 'If plants do not get water, they die.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is 'by + gerund' transformed?

options.A: By + gerund often expresses means
options.B: By + gerund often expresses contrast
options.C: By + gerund often expresses condition
options.D: By + gerund often expresses time

questions.explanation: By + gerund often expresses means: 'By working hard, she succeeded' → 'She worked hard, and therefore she succeeded.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the comparative degree transformed? 'Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.'

options.A: Ravi is the tallest boy in the class.
options.B: Ravi is as tall as any other boy in the class.
options.C: No other boy is taller than Ravi.
options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class' → 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the positive degree transformed into comparative? 'No other boy is as tall as Ravi.'

options.A: Ravi is taller than any other boy.
options.B: Ravi is the tallest boy.
options.C: Ravi is as tall as any other boy.
options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'No other boy is as tall as Ravi' → 'Ravi is taller than any other boy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the superlative degree transformed? 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class.'

options.A: Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.
options.B: Ravi is as tall as any other boy in the class.
options.C: No other boy is tall.
options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class' → 'Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.' These forms require a clearly defined comparison group.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What punctuation is commonly used between independent clauses in a compound sentence?

options.A: A comma before a coordinating conjunction
options.B: An exclamation mark
options.C: A question mark
options.D: A colon only

questions.explanation: A comma before a coordinating conjunction is standard when it joins two independent clauses: 'I called him, but he did not answer.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a semicolon join two closely related independent clauses?

options.A: Yes
options.B: No, only a comma can
options.C: No, only a full stop can
options.D: No, only a conjunction can

questions.explanation: Yes, a semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses: 'The road was blocked; we took another route.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Where is a comma placed in a complex sentence?

options.A: A dependent clause placed before the main clause is commonly followed by a comma
options.B: A dependent clause placed after the main clause is always followed by a comma
options.C: A comma is never used in a complex sentence
options.D: A comma is placed after every word

questions.explanation: A dependent clause placed before the main clause is commonly followed by a comma: 'Although it was late, we continued.' A trailing dependent clause usually does not need a comma: 'We continued although it was late.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a comma splice?

options.A: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma
options.B: Joining two independent clauses with a semicolon
options.C: Joining two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction
options.D: Using a comma after a dependent clause

questions.explanation: A comma splice is joining two independent clauses with only a comma: 'It was late, we went home.' Correct it with a full stop, semicolon or coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a sentence fragment?

options.A: An incomplete sentence presented as a complete one, often a dependent clause without a main clause
options.B: A sentence with two independent clauses
options.C: A sentence with a semicolon
options.D: A sentence with a coordinating conjunction

questions.explanation: A sentence fragment is an incomplete sentence presented as a complete one, often a dependent clause without a main clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is parallel structure?

options.A: Using matching grammatical forms for items in a series or paired construction
options.B: Using different grammatical forms for each item
options.C: Using only nouns in a series
options.D: Using only verbs in a series

questions.explanation: Parallel structure means using matching grammatical forms for items in a series or paired construction: 'She likes reading, writing and singing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is parallelism important in transformation?

options.A: The transformed sentence must keep equivalent grammatical forms and a balanced construction
options.B: It makes the sentence longer
options.C: It changes the meaning
options.D: It removes the need for punctuation

questions.explanation: Parallelism is important in transformation because the transformed sentence must keep equivalent grammatical forms and a balanced construction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Although he was poor, but he was honest.'

options.A: Although he was poor, he was honest. / He was poor, but he was honest.
options.B: Although he was poor, but he was honest.
options.C: Although he was poor and but he was honest.
options.D: Although but he was poor, he was honest.

questions.explanation: Do not normally use although and but together in the same clause structure. Correct forms: 'Although he was poor, he was honest.' / 'He was poor, but he was honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Despite he was ill, he attended class.'

options.A: Despite being ill, he attended class. / Although he was ill, he attended class.
options.B: Despite he was ill, but he attended class.
options.C: Despite of he was ill, he attended class.
options.D: Despite he ill, he attended class.

questions.explanation: Despite is followed by a noun/gerund; although introduces a clause. Correct: 'Despite being ill, he attended class.' / 'Although he was ill, he attended class.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Because of he was late, he missed the bus.'

options.A: Because he was late, he missed the bus.
options.B: Because of he was late, but he missed the bus.
options.C: Because of being he was late, he missed the bus.
options.D: Because of late, he missed the bus.

questions.explanation: Use because + clause; because of + noun/gerund. Correct: 'Because he was late, he missed the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'He is too weak that he cannot walk.'

options.A: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
options.B: He is too weak to cannot walk.
options.C: He is too weak so that he cannot walk.
options.D: He is very weak that he cannot walk.

questions.explanation: Use too...to or so...that. Correct: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'No sooner he arrived than it rained.'

options.A: No sooner had he arrived than it rained.
options.B: No sooner did he arrived than it rained.
options.C: No sooner he had arrived when it rained.
options.D: No sooner had he arrived when it rained.

questions.explanation: Inversion with had follows no sooner in this pattern: 'No sooner had he arrived than it rained.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Hardly had he reached than the train left.'

options.A: Hardly had he reached when the train left.
options.B: Hardly had he reached than the train left.
options.C: Hardly he had reached when the train left.
options.D: Hardly did he reached when the train left.

questions.explanation: Hardly/scarcely generally pair with when; no sooner pairs with than. Correct: 'Hardly had he reached when the train left.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.'

options.A: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.B: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.C: Unless you will hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.D: Unless you are not hurry, you will miss the bus.

questions.explanation: Unless already means if not; avoid the extra negative. Correct: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'He is the most tallest boy.'

options.A: He is the tallest boy.
options.B: He is the most tall boy.
options.C: He is more tallest boy.
options.D: He is tallest the boy.

questions.explanation: Do not combine most and the -est form. Correct: 'He is the tallest boy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'In spite of he worked hard, he failed.'

options.A: In spite of working hard, he failed. / Although he worked hard, he failed.
options.B: In spite of he worked hard, but he failed.
options.C: In spite of he working hard, he failed.
options.D: In spite of worked hard, he failed.

questions.explanation: Use a noun/gerund after in spite of. Correct: 'In spite of working hard, he failed.' / 'Although he worked hard, he failed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Being a rainy day, we stayed home.'

options.A: It being a rainy day, we stayed home. / As it was a rainy day, we stayed home.
options.B: Being a rainy day, but we stayed home.
options.C: Being a rainy day, so we stayed home.
options.D: Being a rainy day, and we stayed home.

questions.explanation: Avoid an unattached participle with the wrong implied subject. Correct: 'It being a rainy day, we stayed home.' / 'As it was a rainy day, we stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'He worked hard and because he passed.'

options.A: He worked hard, so he passed.
options.B: He worked hard and because he passed.
options.C: He worked hard because and he passed.
options.D: He worked hard, and because he passed.

questions.explanation: Do not combine coordinators and subordinators incorrectly. Correct: 'He worked hard, so he passed.'

options.C: Unless you will study, you will fail.
options.D: Unless you are not studying, you will fail.

questions.explanation: 'If you do not study, you will fail' ↔ 'Unless you study, you will fail.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform: 'Although it was raining, we played.' (back to despite)

options.A: Despite the rain, we played.
options.B: Despite it was raining, we played.
options.C: Despite of the rain, we played.
options.D: Despite raining, we played.

questions.explanation: 'Although it was raining, we played' ↔ 'Despite the rain, we played.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform: 'Because he was ill, he was absent.' (back to because of)

options.A: Because of his illness, he was absent.
options.B: Because of he was ill, he was absent.
options.C: Because of being he was ill, he was absent.
options.D: Because of ill, he was absent.

questions.explanation: 'Because he was ill, he was absent' ↔ 'Because of his illness, he was absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform: 'If plants do not get water, they die.' (back to without)

options.A: Without water, plants die.
options.B: Without plants get water, they die.
options.C: Without getting water, plants die.
options.D: Without plants, water dies.

questions.explanation: 'If plants do not get water, they die' ↔ 'Without water, plants die.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform: 'She worked hard, and therefore she succeeded.' (back to by + gerund)

options.A: By working hard, she succeeded.
options.B: By she worked hard, she succeeded.
options.C: By work hard, she succeeded.
options.D: By hard working, she succeeded.

questions.explanation: 'She worked hard, and therefore she succeeded' ↔ 'By working hard, she succeeded.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform the superlative into comparative: 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class.'

options.A: Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.
options.B: Ravi is as tall as any other boy in the class.
options.C: No other boy is tall.
options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class' → 'Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.' These forms require a clearly defined comparison group.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform the comparative into positive degree: 'Ravi is taller than any other boy.'

options.A: No other boy is as tall as Ravi.
options.B: Ravi is the tallest boy.
options.C: Ravi is as tall as any other boy.
options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi is taller than any other boy' → 'No other boy is as tall as Ravi.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform the positive degree into superlative: 'No other metal is as useful as iron.'

options.A: Iron is the most useful metal.
options.B: Iron is more useful than any other metal.
options.C: Iron is as useful as any other metal.
options.D: Iron is not useful.

questions.explanation: 'No other metal is as useful as iron' → 'Iron is the most useful metal.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: because
options.B: for
options.C: nor
options.D: yet

questions.explanation: FANBOYS are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a subordinating conjunction?

options.A: so
options.B: because
options.C: although
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: 'So' is a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). Common subordinators include because, although, if, unless, when, while, before and after.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: because / since / as → so / therefore
options.B: because / since / as → but / yet
options.C: although → so / therefore
options.D: unless → and (imperative + and)

questions.explanation: Reason/result: complex 'because / since / as' → compound 'so / therefore'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: although / though / even though → but / yet / still
options.B: although / though / even though → so / therefore
options.C: if → or / otherwise
options.D: unless → and (imperative + and)

questions.explanation: Contrast/concession: complex 'although / though / even though' → compound 'but / yet / still'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: unless → or / otherwise
options.B: unless → and (imperative + and)
options.C: if → or / otherwise
options.D: when → so / therefore

questions.explanation: Negative condition: complex 'unless' → compound 'or / otherwise'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: if → and (imperative + and)
options.B: if → or / otherwise
options.C: if → but / yet
options.D: if → so / therefore

questions.explanation: Condition: complex 'if' → compound 'and (imperative + and)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: when / after / before → and then / and
options.B: when / after / before → but / yet
options.C: so that → so / therefore
options.D: even though → or / otherwise

questions.explanation: Time: complex 'when / after / before' → compound 'and then / and'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which transformation correctly changes 'He is always punctual' into a negative sentence using 'never'?

options.A: He is never late.
options.B: He is never punctual.
options.C: He is not always punctual.
options.D: He is sometimes late.

questions.explanation: 'He is always punctual' → 'He is never late.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which transformation correctly changes 'Nobody can deny the truth' into an affirmative sentence?

options.A: Everybody must accept the truth.
options.B: Somebody can deny the truth.
options.C: Nobody accepts the truth.
options.D: Everybody can deny the truth.

questions.explanation: 'Nobody can deny the truth' → 'Everybody must accept the truth.' This is a contextual equivalent, not a word-for-word substitution.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following introduces an exclamation of surprise?

options.A: Oh / ah
options.B: Because
options.C: Although
options.D: Unless

questions.explanation: Words commonly introducing exclamations include what, how, alas, hurrah, bravo, oh, ah and expressions such as would that and if only.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following contains a finite verb?

options.A: writes
options.B: to write
options.C: writing
options.D: written

questions.explanation: A finite verb is marked for tense and/or agrees with its subject, e.g. writes, wrote, is, have. 'To write', 'writing' and 'written' are non-finite forms.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-finite verb form?

options.A: to write
options.B: writes
options.C: wrote
options.D: is

questions.explanation: Non-finite verb forms include to write, writing and written. They do not independently show tense or subject agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In simple-to-compound transformation, which coordinator best reflects the causal relation in 'To avoid punishment, he confessed'?

options.A: so
options.B: but
options.C: or
options.D: yet

questions.explanation: 'To avoid punishment, he confessed' → 'He wanted to avoid punishment, so he confessed.' The exact causal relation should be preserved.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In simple-to-compound transformation, which coordinator best reflects the additive relation in 'Besides being intelligent, she is hardworking'?

options.A: and
options.B: but
options.C: or
options.D: so

questions.explanation: 'Besides being intelligent, she is hardworking' → 'She is intelligent, and she is also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In complex-to-compound transformation, which coordinator best reflects the result relation in 'He is so weak that he cannot walk'?

options.A: and
options.B: but
options.C: or
options.D: yet

questions.explanation: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk' → 'He is very weak, and he cannot walk.' This preserves the basic result, though the exact emphasis may differ.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a comma splice?

options.A: It was late, we went home.
options.B: It was late; we went home.
options.C: It was late, so we went home.
options.D: It was late. We went home.

questions.explanation: 'It was late, we went home' joins two independent clauses with only a comma — a comma splice. Correct it with a full stop, semicolon or coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is a sentence fragment?

options.A: Although it was late.
options.B: Although it was late, we continued.
options.C: We continued although it was late.
options.D: It was late, and we continued.

questions.explanation: 'Although it was late' is a dependent clause without a main clause — a sentence fragment.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly demonstrates parallel structure?

options.A: She likes reading, writing and singing.
options.B: She likes reading, to write and singing.
options.C: She likes to read, writing and sing.
options.D: She likes read, writing and singing.

questions.explanation: Parallel structure uses matching grammatical forms for items in a series: 'She likes reading, writing and singing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly places a comma in a complex sentence with a trailing dependent clause?

options.A: We continued although it was late.
options.B: We continued, although it was late.
options.C: We continued although, it was late.
options.D: We continued although it was late,.

questions.explanation: A trailing dependent clause usually does not need a comma: 'We continued although it was late.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly avoids using 'although' and 'but' together?

options.A: Although he was poor, he was honest.
options.B: Although he was poor, but he was honest.
options.C: Although but he was poor, he was honest.
options.D: Although he was poor and but he was honest.

questions.explanation: Do not normally use although and but together in the same clause structure: 'Although he was poor, he was honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'too...to' or 'so...that'?

options.A: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
options.B: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
options.C: He is too weak so that he cannot walk.
options.D: He is very weak that he cannot walk.

questions.explanation: Use too...to or so...that: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'no sooner'?

options.A: No sooner had he arrived than it rained.
options.B: No sooner he arrived than it rained.
options.C: No sooner had he arrived when it rained.
options.D: No sooner did he arrived than it rained.

questions.explanation: Inversion with had follows no sooner in this pattern: 'No sooner had he arrived than it rained.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly pairs 'hardly' with its conjunction?

options.A: Hardly had he reached when the train left.
options.B: Hardly had he reached than the train left.
options.C: Hardly he had reached when the train left.
options.D: Hardly did he reached when the train left.

questions.explanation: Hardly/scarcely generally pair with when; no sooner pairs with than: 'Hardly had he reached when the train left.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'unless' without an extra negative?

options.A: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.B: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.C: Unless you will hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.D: Unless you are not hurry, you will miss the bus.

questions.explanation: Unless already means if not; avoid the extra negative: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly forms the superlative?

options.A: He is the tallest boy.
options.B: He is the most tallest boy.
options.C: He is more tallest boy.
options.D: He is tallest the boy.

questions.explanation: Do not combine most and the -est form: 'He is the tallest boy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'in spite of'?

options.A: In spite of working hard, he failed.
options.B: In spite of he worked hard, he failed.
options.C: In spite of worked hard, he failed.
options.D: In spite of he working hard, he failed.

questions.explanation: Use a noun/gerund after in spite of: 'In spite of working hard, he failed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly avoids an unattached participle?

options.A: It being a rainy day, we stayed home.
options.B: Being a rainy day, we stayed home.
options.C: Being a rainy day, but we stayed home.
options.D: Being a rainy day, so we stayed home.

questions.explanation: Avoid an unattached participle with the wrong implied subject: 'It being a rainy day, we stayed home.' / 'As it was a rainy day, we stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly avoids combining coordinators and subordinators incorrectly?

options.A: He worked hard, so he passed.
options.B: He worked hard and because he passed.
options.C: He worked hard because and he passed.
options.D: He worked hard, and because he passed.

questions.explanation: Do not combine coordinators and subordinators incorrectly: 'He worked hard, so he passed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the absolute construction without an unnecessary conjunction?

options.A: The sun having set, we returned.
options.B: The sun having set, and we returned.
options.C: The sun having set, but we returned.
options.D: The sun having set, so we returned.

questions.explanation: Do not add an unnecessary coordinating conjunction to this simple construction: 'The sun having set, we returned.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which transformation correctly preserves the meaning of 'Who does not know that the Earth is round?'

options.A: Everybody knows that the Earth is round.
options.B: Nobody knows that the Earth is round.
options.C: Somebody knows that the Earth is round.
options.D: Who knows that the Earth is round?

questions.explanation: Check the implied answer and preserve the assertion's meaning: 'Who does not know that the Earth is round?' → 'Everybody knows that the Earth is round.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates an exclamatory sentence?

options.A: What a nice day it is!
options.B: What a nice day it is.
options.C: What a nice day it is?
options.D: What a nice day it is;

questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences normally take an exclamation mark: 'What a nice day it is!'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into negative without changing meaning: 'He is too weak to walk.'

options.B: He is not too weak to walk.
options.C: He is weak enough to walk.
options.D: He is too weak that he cannot walk.

questions.explanation: 'He is too weak to walk' → 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into affirmative: 'He never tells lies.'

options.A: He always speaks the truth.
options.B: He sometimes tells lies.
options.C: He never speaks the truth.
options.D: He often tells lies.

questions.explanation: 'He never tells lies' → 'He always speaks the truth.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into interrogative: 'Everyone respects an honest person.'

options.A: Who does not respect an honest person?
options.B: Does everyone respect an honest person?

options.D: Why does everyone respect an honest person?

questions.explanation: 'Everyone respects an honest person' → 'Who does not respect an honest person?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'What a beautiful painting it is!'

options.A: It is a very beautiful painting.
options.B: What a painting it is.
options.C: The painting is beautiful.
options.D: Is it a beautiful painting?

questions.explanation: 'What a beautiful painting it is!' → 'It is a very beautiful painting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into assertive: 'Alas! The old man is dead.'

options.A: It is very sad that the old man is dead.
options.B: The old man is dead.
options.C: Is the old man dead?
options.D: The old man is not dead.

questions.explanation: 'Alas! The old man is dead' → 'It is very sad that the old man is dead.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'Although he was tired, he continued working.'

options.A: He was tired, but he continued working.
options.B: He was tired, so he continued working.
options.C: He was tired, and he continued working.
options.D: He was tired, or he continued working.

questions.explanation: 'Although he was tired, he continued working' → 'He was tired, but he continued working.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'In spite of his poverty, he is generous.'

options.D: When he is poor, he is generous.

questions.explanation: 'In spite of his poverty, he is generous' → 'Although he is poor, he is generous.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into simple: 'When she saw the teacher, she stood up.'
