options.D: If she saw the teacher, she stood up.

questions.explanation: 'When she saw the teacher, she stood up' → 'On seeing the teacher, she stood up.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'As he was ill, he did not attend school.'

options.A: He was ill, so he did not attend school.
options.B: He was ill, but he did not attend school.
options.C: He was ill, and he did not attend school.
options.D: He was ill, or he did not attend school.

questions.explanation: 'As he was ill, he did not attend school' → 'He was ill, so he did not attend school.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'He is too proud to apologise.'

options.A: He is so proud that he will not apologise.
options.B: He is too proud that he will not apologise.
options.C: He is proud enough to apologise.
options.D: He is not proud to apologise.

questions.explanation: 'He is too proud to apologise' → 'He is so proud that he will not apologise.' Context determines the exact meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change using 'no sooner': 'As soon as the train arrived, the passengers got in.'

options.D: No sooner did the train arrive than the passengers got in.

questions.explanation: 'As soon as the train arrived, the passengers got in' → 'No sooner had the train arrived than the passengers got in.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change using 'unless': 'If you do not work hard, you will not succeed.'

options.A: Unless you work hard, you will not succeed.
options.B: Unless you do not work hard, you will not succeed.

options.D: Unless you are not working hard, you will not succeed.

questions.question: Change into simple: 'Though he was rich, he was unhappy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into complex: 'The girl wearing a blue dress is my sister.'

options.D: The girl when wearing a blue dress is my sister.

questions.explanation: 'The girl wearing a blue dress is my sister' → 'The girl who is wearing a blue dress is my sister.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into compound: 'If you hurry, you will catch the bus.'

options.A: Hurry, and you will catch the bus.
options.B: Hurry, or you will catch the bus.
options.C: Hurry, but you will catch the bus.
options.D: Hurry, so you will catch the bus.

questions.explanation: 'If you hurry, you will catch the bus' → 'Hurry, and you will catch the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into negative: 'Only a fool would believe this.'

options.A: None but a fool would believe this.
options.B: Not a fool would believe this.
options.C: No fool would believe this.
options.D: A fool would not believe this.

questions.explanation: 'Only a fool would believe this' → 'None but a fool would believe this.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into interrogative: 'Nobody can deny the value of education.'

options.A: Who can deny the value of education?
options.B: Can nobody deny the value of education?
options.C: Why can nobody deny the value of education?
options.D: Who cannot deny the value of education?

questions.explanation: 'Nobody can deny the value of education' → 'Who can deny the value of education?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into affirmative: 'No one is free from mistakes.'

options.A: Everyone makes mistakes.
options.B: Someone is free from mistakes.
options.C: No one makes mistakes.
options.D: Everyone is free from mistakes.

questions.explanation: 'No one is free from mistakes' → 'Everyone makes mistakes.' A natural equivalent in general context.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'Although it was raining, we went out.'

options.A: Complex sentence: one main clause and one dependent adverb clause of concession
options.B: Simple sentence
options.C: Compound sentence
options.D: Compound-complex sentence

questions.explanation: 'Although it was raining, we went out' is a complex sentence: one main clause and one dependent adverb clause of concession.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'She opened the door and entered the room.'

options.A: Simple sentence with a compound predicate (one independent clause)
options.B: Compound sentence
options.C: Complex sentence
options.D: Compound-complex sentence

questions.explanation: 'She opened the door and entered the room' is a simple sentence with a compound predicate (one independent clause).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'The bell rang, and the students left.'

options.A: Compound sentence: two independent clauses joined by and
options.B: Simple sentence
options.C: Complex sentence
options.D: Compound-complex sentence

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'I know that he is honest.'

options.A: Complex sentence: the noun clause 'that he is honest' is the object of know
options.B: Simple sentence
options.C: Compound sentence
options.D: Compound-complex sentence

questions.explanation: 'I know that he is honest' is a complex sentence: the noun clause 'that he is honest' is the object of know.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Despite he was tired, he worked.'

options.A: Despite being tired, he worked. / Although he was tired, he worked.
options.B: Despite he was tired, but he worked.
options.C: Despite of he was tired, he worked.
options.D: Despite he tired, he worked.

questions.explanation: 'Despite he was tired, he worked' → 'Despite being tired, he worked.' / 'Although he was tired, he worked.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'No sooner had I reached when it started raining.'

options.A: No sooner had I reached than it started raining.
options.B: No sooner had I reached when it started raining.
options.C: No sooner I had reached than it started raining.
options.D: No sooner did I reached than it started raining.

questions.explanation: 'No sooner had I reached when it started raining' → 'No sooner had I reached than it started raining.' No sooner pairs with than.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct the sentence: 'Unless you do not practise, you cannot improve.'

options.A: Unless you practise, you cannot improve.
options.B: Unless you do not practise, you cannot improve.
options.C: Unless you will practise, you cannot improve.
options.D: Unless you are not practising, you cannot improve.

questions.explanation: 'Unless you do not practise, you cannot improve' → 'Unless you practise, you cannot improve.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What must a transformation preserve?

options.A: The original meaning, tense reference and logical relationship
options.B: Only the number of words
options.C: Only the punctuation
options.D: Only the subject

questions.explanation: Transformation must preserve the original meaning, tense reference and logical relationship.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In affirmative ↔ negative transformation, what should not be confused?

options.A: 'not all' with 'none'
options.B: 'and' with 'but'
options.C: 'who' with 'whom'
options.D: 'simple' with 'compound'

questions.explanation: In affirmative ↔ negative transformation, use logically equivalent expressions; do not confuse 'not all' with 'none'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What do rhetorical questions imply?

options.A: They imply an answer and can express a strong assertion
options.B: They always require a detailed answer
options.C: They have no meaning
options.D: They are always exclamatory

questions.explanation: Rhetorical questions imply an answer and can express a strong assertion.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is an exclamatory sentence changed into an assertive sentence?

options.A: Remove the exclamatory form and express the same feeling as a statement
options.B: Add an exclamation mark
options.C: Change it into a question
options.D: Remove the verb

questions.explanation: Exclamatory → assertive: remove the exclamatory form and express the same feeling as a statement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Match the sentence type: Simple sentence — ?

options.A: One independent clause
options.B: Two or more independent clauses
options.C: One main clause plus at least one dependent clause
options.D: No clause

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Match the sentence type: Compound sentence — ?

options.A: One independent clause
options.B: Two or more independent clauses
options.C: One main clause plus at least one dependent clause
options.D: No clause

questions.explanation: Compound sentence: two or more independent clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Match the sentence type: Complex sentence — ?

options.A: One independent clause
options.B: Two or more independent clauses
options.C: One main clause plus at least one dependent clause
options.D: No clause

questions.explanation: Complex sentence: one main clause plus at least one dependent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What do FANBOYS stand for?

options.A: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
options.B: for, although, nor, but, or, yet, so
options.C: for, and, not, but, or, yet, so
options.D: for, and, nor, because, or, yet, so

questions.explanation: FANBOYS are coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a list of common subordinators?

options.A: because, although, if, unless, when, while, before, after
options.B: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
options.C: who, whom, whose, which, that
options.D: what, how, alas, hurrah, bravo

questions.explanation: Common subordinators include because, although, if, unless, when, while, before and after.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Although/though + ____; despite/in spite of + ____.

options.A: clause; noun or gerund
options.B: noun; clause
options.C: gerund; clause
options.D: phrase; clause

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Because + ____; because of + ____.

options.A: clause; noun or gerund

options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class' → 'Ravi is taller than any other boy in the class.' These forms require a clearly defined comparison group.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform the comparative into positive degree: 'Ravi is taller than any other boy.'

options.A: No other boy is as tall as Ravi.
options.B: Ravi is the tallest boy.
options.C: Ravi is as tall as any other boy.
options.D: Ravi is not tall.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi is taller than any other boy' → 'No other boy is as tall as Ravi.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Transform the positive degree into superlative: 'No other metal is as useful as iron.'

options.A: Iron is the most useful metal.
options.B: Iron is more useful than any other metal.
options.C: Iron is as useful as any other metal.
options.D: Iron is not useful.

questions.explanation: 'No other metal is as useful as iron' → 'Iron is the most useful metal.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: because
options.B: for
options.C: nor
options.D: yet

questions.explanation: FANBOYS are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a subordinating conjunction?

options.A: so
options.B: because
options.C: although
options.D: unless

questions.explanation: 'So' is a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). Common subordinators include because, although, if, unless, when, while, before and after.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: because / since / as → so / therefore
options.B: because / since / as → but / yet
options.C: although → so / therefore
options.D: unless → and (imperative + and)

questions.explanation: Reason/result: complex 'because / since / as' → compound 'so / therefore'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: although / though / even though → but / yet / still
options.B: although / though / even though → so / therefore
options.C: if → or / otherwise
options.D: unless → and (imperative + and)

questions.explanation: Contrast/concession: complex 'although / though / even though' → compound 'but / yet / still'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: unless → or / otherwise
options.B: unless → and (imperative + and)
options.C: if → or / otherwise
options.D: when → so / therefore

questions.explanation: Negative condition: complex 'unless' → compound 'or / otherwise'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: if → and (imperative + and)
options.B: if → or / otherwise
options.C: if → but / yet
options.D: if → so / therefore

questions.explanation: Condition: complex 'if' → compound 'and (imperative + and)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: when / after / before → and then / and
options.B: when / after / before → but / yet
options.C: so that → so / therefore
options.D: even though → or / otherwise

questions.explanation: Time: complex 'when / after / before' → compound 'and then / and'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: so that / in order that → and so / imperative + and (contextual)
options.B: so that → but / yet
options.C: so that → or / otherwise
options.D: so that → so / therefore

questions.explanation: Purpose: complex 'so that / in order that' → compound 'and so / imperative + and (contextual)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: so...that → and therefore / and
options.B: so...that → but / yet
options.C: so...that → or / otherwise
options.D: so...that → and (imperative + and)

questions.explanation: Result: complex 'so...that' → compound 'and therefore / and'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the complex connector with its compound equivalent?

options.A: even though → but / yet
options.B: even though → so / therefore
options.C: even though → and (imperative + and)
options.D: even though → or / otherwise

questions.explanation: Concession: complex 'even though' → compound 'but / yet'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which transformation correctly changes 'He is always punctual' into a negative sentence using 'never'?

options.A: He is never late.
options.B: He is never punctual.
options.C: He is not always punctual.
options.D: He is sometimes late.

questions.explanation: 'He is always punctual' → 'He is never late.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which transformation correctly changes 'Nobody can deny the truth' into an affirmative sentence?

options.A: Everybody must accept the truth.
options.B: Somebody can deny the truth.
options.C: Nobody accepts the truth.
options.D: Everybody can deny the truth.

questions.explanation: 'Nobody can deny the truth' → 'Everybody must accept the truth.' This is a contextual equivalent, not a word-for-word substitution.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following introduces an exclamation of surprise?

options.A: Oh / ah
options.B: Because
options.C: Although
options.D: Unless

questions.explanation: Words commonly introducing exclamations include what, how, alas, hurrah, bravo, oh, ah and expressions such as would that and if only.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following contains a finite verb?

options.A: writes
options.B: to write
options.C: writing
options.D: written

questions.explanation: A finite verb is marked for tense and/or agrees with its subject, e.g. writes, wrote, is, have. 'To write', 'writing' and 'written' are non-finite forms.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-finite verb form?

options.A: to write
options.B: writes
options.C: wrote
options.D: is

questions.explanation: Non-finite verb forms include to write, writing and written. They do not independently show tense or subject agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In simple-to-compound transformation, which coordinator best reflects the causal relation in 'To avoid punishment, he confessed'?

options.A: so
options.B: but
options.C: or
options.D: yet

questions.explanation: 'To avoid punishment, he confessed' → 'He wanted to avoid punishment, so he confessed.' The exact causal relation should be preserved.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In simple-to-compound transformation, which coordinator best reflects the additive relation in 'Besides being intelligent, she is hardworking'?

options.A: and
options.B: but
options.C: or
options.D: so

questions.explanation: 'Besides being intelligent, she is hardworking' → 'She is intelligent, and she is also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In complex-to-compound transformation, which coordinator best reflects the result relation in 'He is so weak that he cannot walk'?

options.A: and
options.B: but
options.C: or
options.D: yet

questions.explanation: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk' → 'He is very weak, and he cannot walk.' This preserves the basic result, though the exact emphasis may differ.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a comma splice?

options.A: It was late, we went home.
options.B: It was late; we went home.
options.C: It was late, so we went home.
options.D: It was late. We went home.

questions.explanation: 'It was late, we went home' joins two independent clauses with only a comma — a comma splice. Correct it with a full stop, semicolon or coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is a sentence fragment?

options.A: Although it was late.
options.B: Although it was late, we continued.
options.C: We continued although it was late.
options.D: It was late, and we continued.

questions.explanation: 'Although it was late' is a dependent clause without a main clause — a sentence fragment.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence demonstrates correct parallel structure?

options.A: She likes reading, writing and singing.
options.B: She likes reading, to write and singing.
options.C: She likes to read, writing and sing.
options.D: She likes read, writing and singing.

questions.explanation: Parallel structure uses matching grammatical forms for items in a series: 'She likes reading, writing and singing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly places a comma in a complex sentence with a trailing dependent clause?

options.A: We continued although it was late.
options.B: We continued, although it was late.
options.C: We continued although, it was late.
options.D: We continued although it was late,.

questions.explanation: A trailing dependent clause usually does not need a comma: 'We continued although it was late.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly avoids using 'although' and 'but' together?

options.A: Although he was poor, he was honest.
options.B: Although he was poor, but he was honest.
options.C: Although but he was poor, he was honest.
options.D: Although he was poor and but he was honest.

questions.explanation: Do not normally use although and but together in the same clause structure: 'Although he was poor, he was honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'too...to' or 'so...that'?

options.A: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
options.B: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
options.C: He is too weak so that he cannot walk.
options.D: He is very weak that he cannot walk.

questions.explanation: Use too...to or so...that: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly pairs 'hardly' with its conjunction?

options.A: Hardly had he reached when the train left.
options.B: Hardly had he reached than the train left.
options.C: Hardly he had reached when the train left.
options.D: Hardly did he reached when the train left.

questions.explanation: Hardly/scarcely generally pair with when; no sooner pairs with than: 'Hardly had he reached when the train left.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'unless' without an extra negative?

options.A: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.B: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.C: Unless you will hurry, you will miss the bus.
options.D: Unless you are not hurry, you will miss the bus.

questions.explanation: Unless already means if not; avoid the extra negative: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly forms the superlative?

options.A: He is the tallest boy.
options.B: He is the most tallest boy.
options.C: He is more tallest boy.
options.D: He is tallest the boy.

questions.explanation: Do not combine most and the -est form: 'He is the tallest boy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'in spite of'?

options.A: In spite of working hard, he failed.
options.B: In spite of he worked hard, he failed.
options.C: In spite of worked hard, he failed.
options.D: In spite of he working hard, he failed.

questions.explanation: Use a noun/gerund after in spite of: 'In spite of working hard, he failed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly avoids an unattached participle?

options.A: It being a rainy day, we stayed home.
options.B: Being a rainy day, we stayed home.
options.C: Being a rainy day, but we stayed home.
options.D: Being a rainy day, so we stayed home.

questions.explanation: Avoid an unattached participle with the wrong implied subject: 'It being a rainy day, we stayed home.' / 'As it was a rainy day, we stayed home.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly avoids combining coordinators and subordinators incorrectly?

options.A: He worked hard, so he passed.
options.B: He worked hard and because he passed.
options.C: He worked hard because and he passed.
options.D: He worked hard, and because he passed.

questions.explanation: Do not combine coordinators and subordinators incorrectly: 'He worked hard, so he passed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the absolute construction without an unnecessary conjunction?

options.A: The sun having set, we returned.
options.B: The sun having set, and we returned.
options.C: The sun having set, but we returned.
options.D: The sun having set, so we returned.

questions.explanation: Do not add an unnecessary coordinating conjunction to this simple construction: 'The sun having set, we returned.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which transformation correctly preserves the meaning of 'Who does not know that the Earth is round?'

options.A: Everybody knows that the Earth is round.
options.B: Nobody knows that the Earth is round.
options.C: Somebody knows that the Earth is round.
options.D: Who knows that the Earth is round?

questions.explanation: Check the implied answer and preserve the assertion's meaning: 'Who does not know that the Earth is round?' → 'Everybody knows that the Earth is round.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates an exclamatory sentence?

options.A: What a nice day it is!
options.B: What a nice day it is.
options.C: What a nice day it is?
options.D: What a nice day it is;

questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences normally take an exclamation mark: 'What a nice day it is!'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which fundamental rule governs every sentence transformation?

options.A: A transformation changes grammatical form while preserving the essential meaning, including subject, tense, time reference, degree of certainty and logical relationship.
options.B: A transformation may freely change the meaning if the grammar is correct.
options.C: A transformation must always shorten the sentence.
options.D: A transformation must always use a question mark.

questions.explanation: The fundamental rule: a transformation changes grammatical form while preserving the essential meaning. The subject, tense, time reference, degree of certainty and logical relationship must remain consistent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When are some transformations possible?

options.A: Only when the context supports them
options.B: Always, regardless of context
options.C: Never
options.D: Only in exclamatory sentences

questions.explanation: Some transformations are possible only when the context supports them.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why can 'He is not a fool' not always be transformed as 'He is wise'?

options.A: Because 'not a fool' does not always mean 'wise'; the best equivalent depends on the intended meaning.
options.B: Because 'not a fool' always means 'wise'.
options.C: Because 'wise' is a negative word.
options.D: Because 'fool' is an adjective.

questions.explanation: The best equivalent depends on the intended meaning; 'not a fool' does not always mean 'wise.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is 'Nobody can deny the truth' → 'Everybody must accept the truth' described as a contextual equivalent?

options.A: Because it is not a word-for-word substitution; it preserves the intended meaning contextually.
options.B: Because it changes the meaning completely.
options.C: Because it uses a double negative.
options.D: Because it is an exclamatory sentence.

questions.explanation: 'Nobody can deny the truth' → 'Everybody must accept the truth' is a contextual equivalent, not a word-for-word substitution.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why does 'Very few cities are as large as Mumbai' → 'Many cities are not as large as Mumbai' depend on the comparison set?

options.A: Because the exact equivalent depends on the comparison set; the intended degree must be preserved.
options.B: Because 'very few' always means 'none'.
options.C: Because 'many' is a negative word.
options.D: Because Mumbai is not a city.

questions.explanation: The exact equivalent depends on the comparison set; preserve the intended degree.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why should a question form not be forced in interrogative transformation?

options.A: Because the transformation must be logically and contextually appropriate; forcing a question form may change the meaning.
options.B: Because interrogative sentences have no meaning.
options.C: Because all statements have natural interrogative equivalents.
options.D: Because rhetorical questions are always wrong.

questions.explanation: Not every statement has a natural interrogative equivalent. The transformation must be logically and contextually appropriate; do not force a question form that changes the meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'May you live long!' → assertive, which construction preserves the blessing or wish?

options.A: I wish that you may live long / I hope that you live long.
options.B: You live long.
options.C: Will you live long?
options.D: You do not live long.

questions.explanation: 'May you live long!' becomes 'I wish that you may live long / I hope that you live long.' Choose the construction that preserves the blessing or wish.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why can a simple sentence contain more than one verb?

options.A: Because it may contain a compound predicate or non-finite verb forms while still having one independent clause.
options.B: Because a simple sentence always has two independent clauses.
options.C: Because a simple sentence has no finite verb.
options.D: Because a simple sentence is always a fragment.

questions.explanation: A simple sentence may contain a compound predicate or non-finite verb forms, while still having one independent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a compound-complex sentence?

options.A: A sentence with two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause
options.B: A sentence with one independent clause only
options.C: A sentence with no finite verb
options.D: A sentence with only non-finite verbs

questions.explanation: A sentence may be compound-complex: it has two or more independent clauses and additional dependent clauses can also occur.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What should be checked in simple-to-compound transformation?

options.A: Ensure each independent clause has a complete subject-finite verb structure and use a coordinator that reflects the original relation
options.B: Only the punctuation
options.C: Only the number of words
options.D: Only the tense of the first clause

questions.explanation: In simple-to-compound transformation, ensure each independent clause has a complete subject-finite verb structure and use a coordinator that reflects the original relation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'He is so weak that he cannot walk' → compound, why may the exact emphasis differ?

options.A: Because the compound form 'He is very weak, and he cannot walk' preserves the basic result but not the exact emphasis.
options.B: Because the meaning is completely changed.
options.C: Because compound sentences cannot express result.
options.D: Because 'so...that' has no equivalent.

questions.explanation: 'He is so weak that he cannot walk' → 'He is very weak, and he cannot walk.' This preserves the basic result, though the exact emphasis may differ.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why are connectors in the conjunction table not universally interchangeable?

options.A: Because each connector preserves a specific logical relation — cause, result, contrast, concession, condition or time.
options.B: Because all connectors mean the same thing.
options.C: Because connectors have no grammatical function.
options.D: Because connectors are only used in exclamatory sentences.

questions.explanation: Connectors in the table are not universally interchangeable. Select the connector that preserves the exact logical relation — cause, result, contrast, concession, condition or time.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the structure of 'no sooner'?

options.A: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple
options.B: No sooner + subject + had + past participle + when + past simple
options.C: No sooner + did + subject + past participle + than + past simple
options.D: No sooner + has + subject + past participle + than + past simple

questions.explanation: The structure is: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple: 'No sooner had I reached than it began to rain.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the structure of 'hardly/scarcely'?

options.A: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when/before + past simple
options.B: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple
options.C: Hardly/Scarcely + did + subject + past participle + when + past simple
options.D: Hardly/Scarcely + has + subject + past participle + than + past simple

questions.explanation: The structure is: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when/before + past simple.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why do degree transformations require a clearly defined comparison group?

options.A: Because comparative, positive and superlative forms depend on a defined set for comparison.
options.B: Because degree transformations never preserve meaning.
options.C: Because all degrees are interchangeable.
options.D: Because degree transformations are exclamatory.

questions.explanation: Comparative, positive and superlative forms require a clearly defined comparison group.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How should a comma splice be corrected?

options.A: With a full stop, semicolon or coordinating conjunction
options.B: By adding another comma
options.C: By removing the verb
options.D: By adding an exclamation mark

questions.explanation: A comma splice is corrected with a full stop, semicolon or coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is parallelism important after transformation?

options.A: The transformed sentence must keep equivalent grammatical forms and a balanced construction.
options.B: It makes the sentence longer.
options.C: It changes the meaning.
options.D: It removes the need for punctuation.

questions.explanation: Parallelism is important in transformation because the transformed sentence must keep equivalent grammatical forms and a balanced construction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why must the tense reference be preserved in a transformation?

options.A: Because a transformation changes grammatical form while preserving the essential meaning, including tense reference.
options.B: Because tense is irrelevant in transformation.
options.C: Because transformation always changes tense.
options.D: Because only exclamatory sentences have tense.

questions.explanation: A transformation changes grammatical form while preserving the essential meaning. The subject, tense, time reference, degree of certainty and logical relationship must remain consistent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why must the degree of certainty be preserved in a transformation?

options.A: Because a transformation must preserve the essential meaning, including the degree of certainty.
options.B: Because certainty is irrelevant to meaning.
options.C: Because transformation always increases certainty.
options.D: Because only interrogative sentences have certainty.

questions.explanation: The subject, tense, time reference, degree of certainty and logical relationship must remain consistent in a transformation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why must the logical relationship be preserved in a transformation?

options.A: Because a transformation must preserve the essential meaning, including the logical relationship between clauses.
options.B: Because logical relationships are irrelevant in grammar.
options.C: Because transformation always changes the logical relationship.
options.D: Because only simple sentences have logical relationships.

questions.explanation: The subject, tense, time reference, degree of certainty and logical relationship must remain consistent in a transformation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'Always' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: Never ... not / never (recast carefully)
options.B: None but
options.C: Not all
options.D: Cannot but

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'Always' becomes 'Never ... not / never (recast carefully)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the negative equivalent of 'Everyone/everybody...' in the affirmative-negative pattern table?

options.A: No one/nobody... not (where logically equivalent)
options.B: None but
options.C: Never
options.D: Cannot but

questions.explanation: In the common affirmative-negative patterns, 'Everyone/everybody...' becomes 'No one/nobody... not (where logically equivalent)'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'It is useless to cry over spilt milk' become in interrogative form?

options.A: What is the use of crying over spilt milk?
options.B: Why is it useful to cry over spilt milk?
options.C: Is it useless to cry over spilt milk?
options.D: Who cries over spilt milk?

questions.explanation: 'It is useless to cry over spilt milk' → 'What is the use of crying over spilt milk?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'There is no use in arguing with him' become in interrogative form?

options.A: What is the use of arguing with him?
options.B: Why argue with him?
options.C: Is there no use in arguing with him?
options.D: Who argues with him?

questions.explanation: 'There is no use in arguing with him' → 'What is the use of arguing with him?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'Everyone loves freedom' become in interrogative form?

options.A: Who does not love freedom?
options.B: Does everyone love freedom?
options.C: Who loves freedom?
options.D: Why does everyone love freedom?

questions.explanation: 'Everyone loves freedom' → 'Who does not love freedom?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'A wise person would never act so foolishly' become in interrogative form?

options.A: Would a wise person ever act so foolishly?
options.B: Would a wise person never act so foolishly?
options.C: Why would a wise person act so foolishly?
options.D: Does a wise person act so foolishly?

questions.explanation: 'A wise person would never act so foolishly' → 'Would a wise person ever act so foolishly?' — a rhetorical question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'Can anyone forget the sacrifice of our soldiers?' become in affirmative form?

options.A: No one can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.
options.B: Everyone can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.
options.C: Anyone can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.
options.D: Someone can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.

questions.explanation: 'Can anyone forget the sacrifice of our soldiers?' → 'No one can forget the sacrifice of our soldiers.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'Would that I were a king!' become in assertive form?

options.A: I wish that I were a king.
options.B: I am a king.
options.C: Am I a king?
options.D: I am not a king.

questions.explanation: 'Would that I were a king!' → 'I wish that I were a king.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'If only I could fly!' become in assertive form?

options.A: I wish I could fly.
options.B: I can fly.
options.C: Can I fly?
options.D: I cannot fly.

questions.explanation: 'If only I could fly!' → 'I wish I could fly.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'What a pity!' become in assertive form?

options.A: It is a great pity.
options.B: It is a pity.
options.C: Is it a pity?
options.D: It is not a pity.

questions.explanation: 'What a pity!' → 'It is a great pity.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Complete the key rule: Simple sentence — one independent clause; compound — two or more independent clauses; complex — ____.

options.A: one main clause plus at least one dependent clause
options.B: one main clause only
options.C: two main clauses only
options.D: no clause at all

questions.explanation: Simple sentence: one independent clause; compound: two or more independent clauses; complex: one main clause plus at least one dependent clause.
